country.name: New Zealand
country.tagline: The world's most southerly wine country, which turned one grape and one valley into a global style in a single generation.

stats.note: Planted area 44,184 ha in 2025 (New Zealand Winegrowers Vineyard Report 2026; 44,229 ha forecast for 2026); production 3.7 mhl in 2025, the second-largest harvest in the country's history (OIV, May 2026).

country.overview:
New Zealand wine is young, cool and astonishingly concentrated. Almost three quarters of the country's 44,000 hectares of vines are in a single region, Marlborough, and about 82 percent of its white plantings are a single grape, Sauvignon Blanc. That combination produced one of the most recognisable wine styles on earth: pungent, zesty Sauvignon smelling of passion fruit, gooseberry, lime and cut grass, made in stainless steel and bottled under screwcap. The country exports about four fifths of its wine, worth around NZ$2 billion a year, and Sauvignon Blanc accounts for most of it.

The speed of the change is the story. Fifty years ago New Zealand made mostly fortified 'sherry' and semi-sweet Müller-Thurgau, much of it in West Auckland sheds run by Croatian (Dalmatian) and Lebanese families. Marlborough had no vineyards until Montana planted at Brancott in 1973, against expert advice that it would be too cold and dry. The first Montana Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc came from the 1979 vintage; Hunter's won a major London tasting in 1986; and Cloudy Bay's first release in 1985, with its misty-mountain label, made the style famous among the world's wine drinkers almost overnight.

But New Zealand is more than Sauvignon. Its Pinot Noir, about three quarters of the red vineyard, ranges from the dark, spicy wines of Central Otago (the world's most southerly commercial wine region, at around 45 degrees south) to the fine, savoury Pinots of Martinborough and North Canterbury. Hawke's Bay, the second-largest region, has warm gravel soils that grow some of the best Syrah and Bordeaux-style blends in the Southern Hemisphere. Chardonnay from Kumeu, Hawke's Bay, Gisborne and Nelson is among the best in the New World. Riesling, Pinot Gris and aromatic whites thrive in Waipara, Nelson and Central Otago, and traditional-method sparkling is growing.

The climate is maritime everywhere. No vineyard is more than about 130 km from the sea, and the westerly winds that cross the Tasman Sea hit the Southern Alps and dump their rain on the West Coast, leaving the eastern side of both islands (where almost all the vineyards are) sunny and relatively dry. Long days, cool nights and high UV light give vivid fruit flavour and high natural acidity; a long, slow ripening season lets aromatics build without the sugar racing ahead.

New Zealand is also a leader in two things the wider wine world cares about. The New Zealand Screwcap Wine Seal Initiative, launched in 2001, made the screwcap the default closure; today almost all New Zealand wine is sealed that way. And Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, started in the mid-1990s, now certifies members that cover about 98 percent of the vineyard area. The registered Geographical Indications are newer: the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006 came into force in 2017, and IPONZ registered the first 18 wine GIs from 2018, adding North Canterbury (2020) and Bannockburn (2022). They are geographic boundaries only, with an 85 percent origin rule, but they finally give names like Marlborough legal protection worldwide.

The country's challenges are the flip side of its success. Reliance on one grape and one market (the United States, Britain and Australia take most exports) leaves it exposed; frost in 2024 and an oversupply of Sauvignon in 2025 hit prices. Growers are planting more Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and talking about sub-regional identity, from Marlborough's Awatere Valley to Central Otago's Bendigo, as the next stage of the story.

history.title: Marsden's vines at Kerikeri
history.text: The Anglican missionary Samuel Marsden planted about 100 vine cuttings at the Kerikeri mission in the Bay of Islands in 1819, the first recorded vines in New Zealand.

history.title: Busby's wine at Waitangi
history.text: James Busby, the British Resident and father of Australian viticulture, planted vines at his house at Waitangi, where the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840. The French explorer Dumont d'Urville tasted his wine there in 1840, the first recorded New Zealand wine.

history.title: Mission Estate
history.text: French Marist missionaries planted vines in Hawke's Bay, settling at Meeanee and later Taradale. Mission Estate, still owned by the Society of Mary, is New Zealand's oldest winery.

history.title: A French miner in Central Otago
history.text: Jean Désiré Feraud, a French gold miner, planted vines at Clyde in Central Otago in 1864; his wine won a prize at a Sydney exhibition in 1881, a century before the region's modern revival.

history.title: Romeo Bragato
history.text: The government invited Romeo Bragato, a Dalmatian-born, Conegliano-trained viticulturist working in Victoria, to assess the colony. He called New Zealand eminently suited to viticulture and warned about phylloxera; as government viticulturist from 1902 he ran the Te Kauwhata research station.

history.title: Dalmatians in West Auckland
history.text: Croatian immigrants from Dalmatia, many of whom came to dig kauri gum, planted small vineyards in Henderson and Kumeu. Babich (1916), Nobilo (1943), Selak, Delegat and the Brajkovich family of Kumeu River built the modern industry from these roots, along with the Lebanese Corban family (1902).

history.title: Prohibition narrowly defeated
history.text: A national referendum voted for prohibition until the votes of soldiers returning from the First World War tipped the result the other way. Licensing laws remained restrictive for decades.

history.title: Montana plants Marlborough
history.text: Frank Yukich's Montana Wines planted the first commercial vineyard in Marlborough at Brancott. Its first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc came from the 1979 vintage.

history.title: Martinborough's terraces
history.text: A 1979 soil and climate report by Dr Derek Milne compared Martinborough to Burgundy. Neil McCallum (Dry River) and Clive Paton (Ata Rangi) planted in 1979 and 1980, and the village became the first centre of New Zealand Pinot Noir.

history.title: Cloudy Bay
history.text: David Hohnen of Cape Mentelle in Margaret River founded Cloudy Bay in Marlborough, with Kevin Judd as winemaker. Its first Sauvignon Blanc, and its label of misty mountains, made Marlborough a world brand.

history.title: Vine-pull scheme
history.text: With a glut of bulk wine, the government paid growers to pull out about a quarter of the national vineyard, mostly Müller-Thurgau. Replanting with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir reset the industry.

history.title: Screwcap initiative
history.text: A group of producers launched the New Zealand Screwcap Wine Seal Initiative to escape cork taint and oxidation. Within a few years almost all New Zealand wine was under screwcap.

history.title: First registered GIs
history.text: Under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006, in force from 2017, IPONZ registered the first New Zealand wine GIs, starting with Marlborough, Hawke's Bay and other regions on 26 February 2018. Bannockburn, registered in 2022, was the most recent.

history.title: Second-largest harvest
history.text: After the frost-hit 2024 vintage, 2025 produced about 3.7 million hectolitres, the second-largest harvest in New Zealand history according to the OIV.

country.classification:
New Zealand's wine Geographical Indications are registered by the Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand (IPONZ) under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006, which came into force in July 2017. There are three 'enduring' GIs created by statute (New Zealand, North Island, South Island) and 19 registered wine GIs: Northland, Auckland (with Matakana, Kumeu and Waiheke Island inside it), Gisborne, Hawke's Bay (with Central Hawke's Bay), Wairarapa (with Gladstone and Martinborough), Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (with North Canterbury, which contains Waipara Valley), Waitaki Valley North Otago and Central Otago (with Bannockburn).

A GI only defines a boundary. To use one on a label, at least 85 percent of the wine must come from the named area (the same 85 percent rule applies to variety and vintage). There are no rules on grape varieties, yields or winemaking. The registration process does require evidence that the area's wines have a quality, reputation or characteristic linked to it, which is why only established places are registered and why informal sub-areas such as Marlborough's Awatere Valley, Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels or Central Otago's Bendigo are not GIs. Gimblett Gravels instead uses a trademark controlled by its winegrowers' association.

Other labelling signals matter more in practice: Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand certification (members cover about 98 percent of vineyard area), organic (BioGro) and biodynamic (Demeter) certification, and in Central Otago and Martinborough the vineyard name.
country.climate_soils:
New Zealand stretches from about 35 degrees south in Northland to 45 degrees south in Central Otago. Every vineyard is close to the sea, but the mountain spine matters more than the coast: the Southern Alps and the North Island's ranges block the prevailing westerlies, so the eastern regions where vines grow are sunny and dry. Marlborough is one of the sunniest places in the country, Central Otago is semi-continental with hot days, freezing nights and frost, while Auckland and Northland are humid and warm.

The country's soils are young and alluvial. Marlborough's Wairau Valley is a bed of greywacke gravels and silts laid down by the Wairau River, with stony, free-draining soils on the north side (Rapaura) and clay-rich soils in the Southern Valleys; the Awatere Valley is higher, colder and windier. Hawke's Bay has deep alluvial gravels left by the Ngaruroro River, notably the Gimblett Gravels, laid bare when a flood in 1867 changed the river's course. Central Otago has schist and windblown loess over gravels. North Canterbury has limestone at Waikari and Weka Pass, a rarity. Nelson's Moutere Hills are weathered gravel-clay. Martinborough sits on a free-draining river terrace of silt over gravel.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: About 82 percent of white plantings and roughly 70 percent of the national vineyard; Marlborough's pungent, aromatic style is the national calling card.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: About 75 percent of red plantings: dark and spicy in Central Otago, savoury in Martinborough, fine and stony in North Canterbury, fragrant in Marlborough's Southern Valleys.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: About 8 percent of whites, but central to New Zealand's fine-wine image: Kumeu River, Hawke's Bay (Te Mata Elston), Gisborne (Millton) and Nelson (Neudorf Moutere).

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.note: About 7 percent of whites, the country's third white, often off-dry in Central Otago and Hawke's Bay.

grapes.name: Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Grown mostly in Hawke's Bay's gravels for Bordeaux-style blends such as Te Mata Coleraine.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: About 6 percent of reds, mostly in Hawke's Bay, where Gimblett Gravels Syrah has a peppery, northern-Rhône profile.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: A small share but a high reputation in Waipara, Central Otago, Marlborough and Nelson, from dry to botrytised.

regions.name: North Island
regions.tagline: The warmer island: Hawke's Bay reds, Kumeu Chardonnay, Martinborough Pinot and the vineyards where New Zealand wine began.
regions.summary: The North Island has about 7,500 ha of vines, about 17 percent of the national total in 2025, but most of the country's wine history and its warmest regions. Hawke's Bay, the largest, grows Bordeaux varieties and Syrah in gravel; Gisborne is the Chardonnay capital; Auckland and its sub-regions (Kumeu, Matakana, Waiheke Island) have the oldest family wineries; and the Wairarapa, at the southern tip, holds Martinborough, an early home of New Zealand Pinot Noir.
regions.history: Samuel Marsden planted the first vines at Kerikeri in 1819, James Busby made the first recorded wine at Waitangi in the 1830s, and French missionaries founded Mission Estate in Hawke's Bay in 1851. West Auckland was the centre of the twentieth-century industry, built by Dalmatian and Lebanese immigrant families.
regions.terroir: Warmer and more humid than the South Island, especially in Northland and Auckland. Hawke's Bay and Gisborne, on the east coast, are sheltered by ranges. Soils range from Auckland's heavy clays to Hawke's Bay's free-draining gravels and Martinborough's river terraces.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris.
regions.styles: Bordeaux blends and Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, aromatic whites.
regions.classification: Enduring GI 'North Island'; registered GIs Northland, Auckland (Matakana, Kumeu, Waiheke Island), Gisborne, Hawke's Bay (Central Hawke's Bay), Wairarapa (Gladstone, Martinborough).

sources.title: IPONZ, Geographical Indications Register (New Zealand wine GIs, registration dates and numbers)
New Zealand Winegrowers, Vineyard Report 2026 (2025 Biosecurity Vineyard Register)

regions.name: South Island
regions.tagline: Four fifths of New Zealand's vines, from the Sauvignon flats of Marlborough to the schist hills of Central Otago.
regions.summary: The South Island has about 36,700 ha of vines, about 83 percent of the national vineyard in 2025, almost all on the dry east side of the Southern Alps. Marlborough alone has 32,000 ha. Further south, Nelson, North Canterbury, Waitaki Valley and Central Otago are smaller, cooler and more varied, and produce much of the country's best Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling.
regions.history: Viticulture began with French settlers at Akaroa (1840) and gold-rush miners in Central Otago (1860s), but the modern South Island industry dates from the 1970s: Montana's Marlborough plantings (1973), Neudorf in Nelson (1978), St Helena and Pegasus Bay in Canterbury, and Rippon and Gibbston Valley in Central Otago.
regions.terroir: Cooler than the North Island, with very high sunshine hours and large day-night temperature swings. Soils include Marlborough's alluvial gravels, Nelson's Moutere clays, North Canterbury's limestone and Central Otago's schist and loess.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Aromatic Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, dry to sweet Riesling, sparkling.
regions.classification: Enduring GI 'South Island'; registered GIs Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury (North Canterbury, Waipara Valley), Waitaki Valley North Otago, Central Otago (Bannockburn).

nz-auckland.name: Auckland
nz-auckland.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Gris
nz-auckland.summary: The Auckland GI covers New Zealand's largest city and its surrounding countryside, with only about 250 ha of vines but many of the country's biggest wine companies' headquarters. It was the heart of twentieth-century New Zealand wine, when Dalmatian, Lebanese and English families made fortified and table wine in Henderson, Kumeu and Huapai. It contains three sub-GIs: Matakana to the north, Kumeu to the north-west and Waiheke Island in the Hauraki Gulf.
nz-auckland.terroir: Warm, humid and wet (more than 1,200 mm of rain a year), on heavy clay soils; vineyards favour slopes and free-draining sites.

nz-bannockburn.name: Bannockburn
nz-bannockburn.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris
nz-bannockburn.summary: The most recent New Zealand wine GI, registered in February 2022, covering a small, warm sub-region of Central Otago on the southern bank of the Kawarau River near Cromwell. Gold miners sluiced its hills in the 1860s and 1870s, leaving the 'Cairnmuir' sluicings, an eerie landscape of cliffs and tailings. Stewart Elms planted Felton Road here in 1991 and 1992; with Mount Difficulty, Akarua and Carrick it made Bannockburn's ripe, structured, mineral Pinot Noir the most celebrated in the region.
nz-bannockburn.terroir: One of the warmest and driest corners of Central Otago, on schist-derived gravels, loess and clays over sandstone, at about 220 to 400 m.
nz-bannockburn.nerd_note: Felton Road's Block 3 and Block 5 Pinot Noirs come from parcels of the original Elms planting, on deeper loess and on a more exposed terrace respectively.

nz-canterbury.name: Canterbury
nz-canterbury.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay
nz-canterbury.summary: The Canterbury GI covers the broad province around Christchurch, from the Canterbury Plains to Banks Peninsula. French settlers planted vines at Akaroa in 1840, and Lincoln University's research in the 1970s showed the plains could ripen cool-climate grapes. Today almost all quality vineyards are in North Canterbury, a separate GI inside it.
nz-canterbury.terroir: Cool, dry and windy, with the nor'wester (a hot, dry foehn wind) a defining feature.

nz-central-hawkes-bay.name: Central Hawke's Bay
nz-central-hawkes-bay.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris
nz-central-hawkes-bay.summary: The southern, cooler part of Hawke's Bay around Waipukurau and Waipawa, registered as its own GI in 2019. It has only a few vineyards, but its limestone hills and cooler climate suit Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.
nz-central-hawkes-bay.terroir: Cooler and more continental than the Heretaunga Plains, with limestone and clay soils.
nz-central-hawkes-bay.nerd_note: Lime Rock Wines takes its name from the limestone outcrops of its vineyard near Waipawa.

nz-central-otago.name: Central Otago
nz-central-otago.grapes: Pinot Noir (about 70 to 80 percent), Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
nz-central-otago.summary:
Central Otago is the world's most southerly commercial wine region, at around 45 degrees south, and its Pinot Noir is New Zealand's most famous red. It is a dramatic place: dry brown hills of schist, rivers and lakes, gold-rush ruins and snow-capped mountains. Jean Désiré Feraud planted vines at Clyde in 1864, but the modern industry began in the 1970s and 1980s with Rolfe and Lois Mills at Rippon on Lake Wanaka (1975) and Alan Brady at Gibbston Valley (first commercial wine in 1987). It now has about 2,100 ha and more than 230 vineyards.

The climate is semi-continental: hot, dry summer days, cold nights and frost in spring and autumn, so vineyards occupy slopes and terraces that drain cold air. Pinot Noir here is vivid and dark-fruited, with spice and fine tannin. Sub-regions differ. Gibbston, in the Kawarau Gorge near Queenstown, is the coolest and highest; Bannockburn (a registered GI since 2022) and the Cromwell Basin (Bendigo, Pisa, Lowburn) are the warmest and give the most powerful wines; Alexandra is dry and continental; Wanaka is lakeside and cool. Felton Road (Bannockburn), Rippon (Wanaka), Burn Cottage, Prophet's Rock (Bendigo) and Two Paddocks are among the leaders.
nz-central-otago.terroir: Schist-derived gravels and loess (windblown silt), very low rainfall (often under 400 mm), high sunshine and big temperature swings. Most vineyards are irrigated.
nz-central-otago.nerd_note: Rippon's vineyard on the shore of Lake Wanaka is one of the most photographed in the world; Nick Mills farms it biodynamically.

nz-gisborne.name: Gisborne
nz-gisborne.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Gewürztraminer
nz-gisborne.summary: Gisborne, on the East Cape, is one of the first places in the world to see the sun each day and calls itself New Zealand's Chardonnay capital. Its fertile alluvial plains grew much of the country's bulk white in the 1970s and 1980s; today its 1,300 ha supply Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and sparkling base, and a few artisans prove its quality. James and Annie Millton started New Zealand's first certified organic and later biodynamic estate here in 1984; their Clos de Ste Anne Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay are reference wines.
nz-gisborne.terroir: Warm, sunny and relatively humid; fertile silty loams on the Poverty Bay flats, with clay-limestone hillsides at Manutuke.
nz-gisborne.nerd_note: Matawhero's Gewürztraminer in the 1970s and 1980s, made by Denis Irwin, was one of the first New Zealand wines to win international praise.

nz-gladstone.name: Gladstone
nz-gladstone.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling
nz-gladstone.summary: A tiny rural district in the Ruamahanga River valley between Martinborough and Masterton, registered in 2019. A handful of family vineyards make Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir on gravelly river terraces.
nz-gladstone.terroir: Alluvial gravels and silts on terraces of the Ruamahanga River; slightly cooler and wetter than Martinborough.
nz-gladstone.nerd_note: Urlar is one of the few Wairarapa estates with organic and biodynamic certification.

nz-hawkes-bay.name: Hawke's Bay
nz-hawkes-bay.grapes: Merlot, Chardonnay, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris
nz-hawkes-bay.summary:
Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's second-largest wine region (about 4,600 ha) and its oldest continuously producing one: French Marist missionaries planted vines in 1851 and their Mission Estate still makes wine at Taradale. It is the country's red-wine heartland, making Bordeaux-style blends of Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc and, increasingly, peppery Syrah, as well as rich Chardonnay.

The key to its reds is gravel. The Gimblett Gravels, about 800 ha of stony former riverbed west of Hastings, were exposed when a great flood in 1867 diverted the Ngaruroro River. Once considered worthless (a concrete company wanted to quarry them), they absorb daytime heat and drain freely, ripening Syrah and Cabernet in a cool climate; producers formed the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowers Association and trademarked the name in 2001. The Bridge Pa Triangle to the south, on red metal soils, and the limestone hills around Havelock North (home of Te Mata Estate, founded in 1896) are the other key districts. Te Mata's Coleraine blend, first made in 1982, is New Zealand's most famous red.
nz-hawkes-bay.terroir: Sunny and dry for the North Island, sheltered from westerlies by the Ruahine and Kaweka ranges. Soils range from free-draining alluvial gravels (Gimblett Gravels, Bridge Pa) to silt loams and limestone hills.
nz-hawkes-bay.nerd_note: Alan Limmer planted Syrah at Stonecroft in the Gimblett Gravels area in 1984 and released its first Syrah from the 1989 vintage, the first modern New Zealand Syrah on the market.

nz-kumeu.name: Kumeu
nz-kumeu.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Merlot
nz-kumeu.summary: Kumeu, with neighbouring Huapai and Waimauku north-west of Auckland, is where Dalmatian families such as the Brajkoviches (Kumeu River), Nobilos and Selaks built wineries from the 1930s and 1940s. Its fame today rests on Chardonnay: Kumeu River, run by Michael Brajkovich (New Zealand's first Master of Wine, 1989) and his family, makes some of the finest Chardonnays in the New World, especially the single-vineyard Maté's and Hunting Hill.
nz-kumeu.terroir: Heavy clay soils over sandstone that retain water in a wet climate; humid summers favour early-ripening varieties and careful canopy work.
nz-kumeu.nerd_note: Kumeu River's Maté's Vineyard, planted in 1990, is named after Maté Brajkovich, who arrived from Dalmatia and bought the property in 1944.

nz-marlborough.name: Marlborough
nz-marlborough.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc (about 80 percent), Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling
nz-marlborough.summary:
Marlborough, at the north-eastern tip of the South Island, has about 32,000 ha of vines, 73 percent of New Zealand's vineyard, and more than 1,100 vineyards. Sheep grazed its flat Wairau Valley until 1973, when Montana planted vines at Brancott against advice that the region was too cold and dry. Its first Sauvignon Blanc, from the 1979 vintage, showed something new: intensely aromatic wine, with passion fruit, gooseberry and fresh-cut grass, and searing acidity. Hunter's success in London in 1986 and Cloudy Bay's launch in 1985 brought world attention, and Marlborough Sauvignon became one of the most successful wine styles of the modern era.

The region has three main sub-areas. The Wairau Valley, along the Wairau River, has stony, free-draining alluvial soils on its northern side (Rapaura) that give the classic tropical style. The Southern Valleys (Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Ben Morven, Waihopai), on clay-rich soils, give more textured Sauvignon, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. The Awatere Valley to the south-east, higher, windier and cooler, gives a leaner, more herbaceous and saline style. Producers such as Dog Point, Greywacke, Clos Henri, Te Whare Ra, Seresin and Churton show that Marlborough can also make complex, barrel-fermented and wild-yeast Sauvignon, serious Pinot Noir and traditional-method sparkling. The flip side is heavy reliance on one grape: the region produced a record crop in 2025 and growers face pressure to diversify.
nz-marlborough.terroir: Very sunny (about 2,400 hours a year), dry (about 650 mm of rain) and with big swings between warm days and cool nights. Soils are young alluvial gravels, silts and clays laid down by the Wairau, Awatere and their tributaries.
nz-marlborough.nerd_note: Ivan Sutherland and James Healy, who left Cloudy Bay to found Dog Point, make Section 94, a barrel-fermented Sauvignon Blanc named after a land-survey section.

nz-martinborough.name: Martinborough
nz-martinborough.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Syrah
nz-martinborough.summary: A small village laid out in the shape of a Union Jack in the 1870s, now one of New Zealand's most important Pinot Noir districts. In 1979 a report by soil scientist Dr Derek Milne compared its climate and free-draining terrace soils to Burgundy; Neil McCallum (Dry River) and Clive Paton (Ata Rangi) planted that year and the next, followed by Martinborough Vineyard and Palliser. Their Pinots, savoury, firm and long-lived, set the standard for New Zealand red in the 1990s. Ata Rangi's Pinot Noir, from the 'Abel' clone said to have been smuggled in from Burgundy, is the region's icon.
nz-martinborough.terroir: The Martinborough Terrace, an old river terrace of silt over deep, free-draining gravel; dry, windy and cool, with frost risk. The Te Muna Road area to the south-east has similar soils.
nz-martinborough.nerd_note: The 'Abel' or 'Gumboot' clone of Pinot Noir is said to have been confiscated from a traveller's gumboot at Auckland airport by customs officer Malcolm Abel, who propagated it.

nz-matakana.name: Matakana
nz-matakana.grapes: Pinot Gris, Syrah, Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
nz-matakana.summary: A small district about an hour north of Auckland, around the village of Matakana and the Mahurangi coast. The first modern vineyards were planted in the 1960s and 1970s, and today about a dozen boutique producers make Bordeaux blends, Syrah, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay for the weekend visitors from the city.
nz-matakana.terroir: Clay soils over sandstone on rolling hills, with warm, humid summers moderated by sea breezes from both coasts.
nz-matakana.nerd_note: Matakana's vineyards share the district with olive groves and a Saturday farmers' market that draws Aucklanders north.

nz-nelson.name: Nelson
nz-nelson.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling
nz-nelson.summary: Nelson, at the top of the South Island, is one of the sunniest places in New Zealand and a small, artistic wine region of about 970 ha. It has two distinct areas: the Waimea Plains, with stony alluvial soils that give fresh Sauvignon and aromatic whites, and the Moutere Hills, where clay-bound gravels give richer Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. German settlers planted vines in the 1840s; the modern era began with Hermann Seifried (1973) and Tim and Judy Finn at Neudorf (1978), whose Moutere Chardonnay is one of the country's best.
nz-nelson.terroir: Sheltered by mountains on three sides; high sunshine and moderate rain. Moutere gravel-clays (weathered, iron-rich) contrast with the stony Waimea Plains.
nz-nelson.nerd_note: Neudorf's Moutere Chardonnay comes from vines on the clay-gravel 'Moutere Gravels', which hold water and give a dense, mineral wine.

nz-new-zealand.name: New Zealand
nz-new-zealand.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
nz-new-zealand.summary: The national GI, created by statute as an 'enduring' GI and registered in July 2017. It covers any wine of which at least 85 percent comes from New Zealand, typically blends across regions.

nz-north-canterbury.name: North Canterbury
nz-north-canterbury.grapes: Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
nz-north-canterbury.summary: North Canterbury, registered in 2020, covers the hills north of Christchurch, including the Waipara Valley and the limestone country around Waikari. With about 1,540 ha, it is a source of some of New Zealand's most intellectually interesting wines: Pyramid Valley's and Bell Hill's limestone-grown Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and Pegasus Bay's Riesling and Pinot.
nz-north-canterbury.terroir: Warm, dry summers and long autumns protected from easterly sea breezes by the Teviotdale Hills; limestone, clay and gravels.
nz-north-canterbury.nerd_note: The limestone at Waikari and Weka Pass is rare in New Zealand, which is one reason Burgundy-obsessed growers chose it.

nz-north-island.name: North Island
nz-north-island.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Syrah, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc
nz-north-island.summary: An enduring GI covering the North Island, used for blends of North Island regions (for example Hawke's Bay and Gisborne fruit). The North Island had about 7,500 ha of vines in 2025, about 17 percent of the national total, led by Hawke's Bay and Gisborne.

nz-northland.name: Northland
nz-northland.summary: New Zealand's northernmost and warmest wine region, and its first: Samuel Marsden planted vines at Kerikeri in 1819 and James Busby made wine at Waitangi in the 1830s. Today about 70 ha of vines support small producers making Syrah, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris in a subtropical, humid climate where no point is more than 50 km from the sea.
nz-northland.terroir: Warm, humid and wet, with clay soils; disease pressure is the main challenge.
nz-northland.nerd_note: Karikari Estate on the Karikari Peninsula is one of the northernmost vineyards in the country.

nz-south-island.name: South Island
nz-south-island.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
nz-south-island.summary: An enduring GI covering the South Island, used for blends such as Marlborough and Nelson or Central Otago and Waitaki fruit. The South Island had about 36,700 ha of vines in 2025, about 83 percent of the national total, most of them in Marlborough.

nz-waiheke-island.name: Waiheke Island
nz-waiheke-island.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
nz-waiheke-island.summary: A hilly island in the Hauraki Gulf, a 40-minute ferry ride from downtown Auckland, which since the 1980s has become a source of expensive Bordeaux blends and Syrah. Goldwater Estate planted the first modern vineyard in 1978 and Stephen White's Stonyridge (1981) made its Larose blend a cult wine. The island is warmer and drier than mainland Auckland, and now has about 30 wineries alongside its holiday homes.
nz-waiheke-island.terroir: Clay over weathered greywacke on steep slopes; warm and maritime, with lower rainfall than Auckland.
nz-waiheke-island.nerd_note: Destiny Bay sells its Bordeaux blends at prices among the highest in New Zealand.

nz-waipara-valley.name: Waipara Valley
nz-waipara-valley.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay
nz-waipara-valley.summary: A small, warm valley about an hour north of Christchurch, registered as a GI in 2018 and sitting within North Canterbury. Pegasus Bay, founded by the Donaldson family in 1985, made its name for Riesling (in dry to botrytised styles) and Pinot Noir; Black Estate, Greystone and Mountford followed. The valley is sheltered from cool easterlies by the Teviotdale Hills, so it ripens grapes well for its latitude.
nz-waipara-valley.terroir: Glacial gravels and clay loams on the valley floor, with limestone-rich clays on the slopes; hot dry summers and the nor'wester wind.

nz-wairarapa.name: Wairarapa
nz-wairarapa.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Syrah
nz-wairarapa.summary: The Wairarapa lies an hour north-east of Wellington across the Remutaka Range and holds about 1,190 ha of vines, mostly Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc. It contains two registered sub-GIs, Martinborough and Gladstone, and the area around Masterton (Opaki). Boutique producers dominate; the region makes only about 3 percent of New Zealand's wine but a much larger share of its fine Pinot.
nz-wairarapa.terroir: A rain shadow behind the Remutaka and Tararua ranges, with strong north-westerly winds that cut yields and keep disease low. Free-draining river-terrace soils over gravel.

nz-waitaki-valley-north-otago.name: Waitaki Valley North Otago
nz-waitaki-valley-north-otago.grapes: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Chardonnay
nz-waitaki-valley-north-otago.summary: One of New Zealand's newest and most marginal regions, in the Waitaki River valley around Kurow and Duntroon, registered in 2018. Its first vines went in around 2001. Limestone outcrops and a cold, frost-prone climate attracted growers such as Jim Jerram (Ostler) and Michelle Richardson. With fewer than 50 ha, it makes taut Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
nz-waitaki-valley-north-otago.terroir: Limestone and schist gravels with windblown loess; very cool, with a short season and frost risk.

sites.name: Waitangi Treaty Grounds
sites.text: James Busby, British Resident from 1833, planted vines beside his house at Waitangi, where the Treaty of Waitangi was signed on 6 February 1840. The French explorer Dumont d'Urville tasted Busby's wine here that year and described a light, sparkling white: the first recorded New Zealand wine. The house is now part of the Treaty Grounds.

sites.name: Kerikeri Mission Station
sites.text: Samuel Marsden, the Anglican missionary, planted about 100 vine cuttings at the Kerikeri mission in 1819, the first recorded in New Zealand. The mission's Kemp House (1822) is the country's oldest surviving building.

sites.name: Mission Estate
sites.text: French Marist missionaries planted vines in Hawke's Bay in 1851 and moved to this hillside at Taradale in 1880. Mission Estate is New Zealand's oldest winery still under the same ownership, the Society of Mary; its seminary building now houses a restaurant.

sites.name: Church Road
sites.text: Founded in 1897 by Bartholomew Steinmetz, a Luxembourger who had worked at the Mission, and later run by Tom McDonald, whose Cabernet in the 1940s and 1950s was one of New Zealand's first serious reds. Pernod Ricard's Church Road now makes Bordeaux blends and Chardonnay here.

sites.name: Te Mata Estate
sites.text: Founded in 1896 by Bernard Chambers on the limestone hills of Havelock North, Te Mata is New Zealand's oldest winery in continuous production. John Buck and Michael Morris bought it in 1974; their Coleraine, a Cabernet-Merlot blend first made in 1982, is the country's most celebrated red, and Elston is a benchmark Chardonnay.

sites.name: Craggy Range
sites.text: Terry Peabody, an Australian businessman, founded Craggy Range in 1997 with viticulturist Steve Smith MW, at the foot of Te Mata Peak. It farms vineyards in the Gimblett Gravels (Sophia, Le Sol Syrah) and at Te Muna Road in Martinborough.

sites.name: Gimblett Gravels
sites.text: About 800 ha of stony former riverbed west of Hastings, exposed when a great flood in 1867 shifted the Ngaruroro River. The gravels store heat and drain freely, ripening Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet. Its winegrowers trademarked the name in 2001 and only wines with 95 percent Gimblett Gravels fruit may use it.

sites.name: Bridge Pa Triangle
sites.text: A triangle of land south of the Gimblett Gravels around the village of Bridge Pa, on 'red metal' soils (iron-stained gravels) and silt loams. It ripens Merlot and Syrah with a softer, more fragrant profile than the gravels and has organised itself as a wine district.

sites.name: Stonecroft
sites.text: Alan Limmer, a soil scientist, planted Syrah at Stonecroft in 1984 and released New Zealand's first modern Syrah from the 1989 vintage, starting the variety's rise in Hawke's Bay.

sites.name: Trinity Hill
sites.text: Founded in 1993 by John Hancock with London restaurateurs Robert and Robyn Wilson. Trinity Hill was one of the first to plant on Gimblett Road and helped create the Gimblett Gravels district; its Homage Syrah is a benchmark.

sites.name: Babich Wines
sites.text: Josip Babich, a Dalmatian immigrant, made his first wine in 1916 in Northland and moved to Henderson in 1919. The family still runs the business, one of the oldest of the West Auckland Croatian wineries.

sites.name: Kumeu River
sites.text: The Brajkovich family bought this Kumeu property in 1944. Michael Brajkovich, New Zealand's first Master of Wine (1989), transformed it into one of the world's great Chardonnay producers; Maté's Vineyard, planted in 1990, is named after his father.

sites.name: Stonyridge
sites.text: Stephen White planted Stonyridge at Onetangi on Waiheke Island in 1981. Its Larose, a Bordeaux-style blend, became one of New Zealand's most sought-after reds and made the island a wine destination.

sites.name: Man O' War
sites.text: A large estate on the remote eastern end of Waiheke Island, on land named after Captain Cook's search for masts. Its vineyards spread across steep slopes and coves facing the Hauraki Gulf.

sites.name: Millton Vineyards
sites.text: James and Annie Millton founded their estate at Manutuke near Gisborne in 1984; it became New Zealand's first certified organic winery and later biodynamic. Clos de Ste Anne, on a steep clay-limestone hill, gives Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Syrah of real distinction.

sites.name: Ata Rangi
sites.text: Clive Paton planted Ata Rangi on a stony former sheep paddock at Martinborough in 1980. Its Pinot Noir, built on the 'Abel' clone, is one of New Zealand's most admired reds; the name means 'new beginning' or 'dawn sky' in Māori.

sites.name: Dry River
sites.text: Neil and Dawn McCallum planted Dry River in 1979 after Derek Milne's report on Martinborough. Their Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer and Riesling, made to age, became some of New Zealand's most collected wines.

sites.name: Escarpment
sites.text: Larry McKenna, often called the 'Prince of Pinot' for his work at Martinborough Vineyard, founded Escarpment on Te Muna Road in 1999, making single-vineyard Pinot Noirs from old Martinborough sites.

sites.name: Neudorf Vineyards
sites.text: Tim and Judy Finn planted Neudorf in the Moutere Hills of Nelson in 1978. Its Moutere Chardonnay, from clay-gravel soils, is one of New Zealand's finest, and the estate now belongs to a group led by Tim and Judy's daughter and partners.

sites.name: Brancott Estate
sites.text: Montana Wines planted the first commercial vineyard in Marlborough here in 1973. The first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc followed in 1979. Now owned by Pernod Ricard and renamed Brancott Estate, its hilltop heritage centre overlooks the vineyards where the style was born.

sites.name: Cloudy Bay
sites.text: David Hohnen of Cape Mentelle founded Cloudy Bay in 1985 with winemaker Kevin Judd, naming it after the bay Captain Cook named in 1770. Its Sauvignon Blanc and misty-mountain label made Marlborough famous worldwide; Te Koko, a barrel-fermented Sauvignon, showed another side. LVMH owns it.

sites.name: Wairau Valley
sites.text: The broad, flat heart of Marlborough along the Wairau River. Its northern side around Rapaura has stony, free-draining alluvial soils (called 'stoney' by locals) that give the classic tropical, pungent Sauvignon Blanc.

sites.name: Southern Valleys
sites.text: A series of side valleys south of the Wairau (Brancott, Omaka, Fairhall, Ben Morven, Waihopai), with clay-rich soils that give more textured Sauvignon Blanc and Marlborough's best Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Awatere Valley
sites.text: A higher, windier and cooler valley south-east of the Wairau around Seddon, planted on a large scale only from the late 1990s. Its Sauvignon Blanc is leaner and more herbal, with tomato-leaf and saline notes.

sites.name: Yealands Estate
sites.text: Peter Yealands planted his estate near the coast at Seaview in the Awatere Valley from 2003, terracing hills with bulldozers. It markets itself on sustainability, including grazing miniature sheep in the vines.

sites.name: Pyramid Valley
sites.text: Mike and Claudia Weersing planted Pyramid Valley in 2000 on limestone near Waikari after a long search for the right soil. Their biodynamic, block-named Pinot Noirs and Chardonnays were acclaimed; Brian Sheth and Steve Smith bought the estate in 2017.

sites.name: Bell Hill
sites.text: Marcel Giesen and Sherwyn Veldhuizen planted Bell Hill on an old limestone quarry at Weka Pass in 1997, densely, Burgundy-style. Its tiny production of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay is among New Zealand's most collected.

sites.name: Pegasus Bay
sites.text: The Donaldson family (neurologist Ivan Donaldson and his wife Christine) planted Pegasus Bay in the Waipara Valley in 1985. Its Rieslings, from dry to the botrytised Aria, and its Pinot Noir made Waipara's reputation.

sites.name: Rippon
sites.text: Rolfe and Lois Mills planted Rippon on the shore of Lake Wanaka in 1975, one of the first modern vineyards in Central Otago. Their son Nick Mills, who trained in Burgundy, farms it biodynamically; the view across the lake to the mountains is one of the most photographed in wine.

sites.name: Felton Road
sites.text: Stewart Elms planted Felton Road at Bannockburn in 1991 and 1992; Englishman Nigel Greening bought it in 2000, and Blair Walter has made the wines since the start. Its biodynamic, block-designated Pinot Noir (Block 3, Block 5, Calvert, Cornish Point) is the benchmark for Central Otago.

sites.name: Gibbston Valley Winery
sites.text: Alan Brady, a journalist from Northern Ireland, planted vines in the Kawarau Gorge in 1981 and released Gibbston Valley's first commercial wine in 1987. Its schist cave, dug into the hill in 1995, is a tourist landmark.

sites.name: Chard Farm
sites.text: Rob and Greg Hay planted Chard Farm on a ledge above the Kawarau Gorge in 1987, reached by a cliff-edge road; it is one of the pioneers of Central Otago Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Bendigo
sites.text: A former gold-mining settlement on the eastern side of Lake Dunstan, now one of Central Otago's warmest districts, with north-facing schist terraces planted since the late 1990s. Prophet's Rock, Quartz Reef and Mount Edward have vineyards here.

sites.name: Gibbston
sites.text: The coolest and highest of Central Otago's sub-regions, along the Kawarau Gorge near Queenstown at up to about 420 m, where Pinot Noir is lighter and more perfumed.

sites.name: Cromwell Basin (Lowburn and Pisa)
sites.text: The broad basin around Lake Dunstan and Cromwell, including Lowburn and the Pisa terraces on the west bank, holds the largest share of Central Otago's vines. It is warm and dry, and gives ripe, dark-fruited Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Alexandra
sites.text: The southernmost Central Otago sub-region, around the town of Alexandra in the Clutha Valley, among the driest places in New Zealand, with large daily temperature swings. Grasshopper Rock, Two Paddocks and Black Ridge make wine here.

sites.name: Burn Cottage
sites.text: A Pinot Noir estate at Lowburn in the Cromwell Basin, founded by the American Sauvage family in 2002 and farmed biodynamically from the start. Ted Lemon of Littorai advises on the wines, which are among the most structured and age-worthy from Central Otago.

sites.name: Te Kauwhata Viticultural Research Station
sites.text: The government research station where Romeo Bragato worked as the first government viticulturist from 1902, testing grape varieties and phylloxera-resistant rootstocks. It shaped New Zealand viticulture for most of the twentieth century.
